extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of scientific method; philosophers of science; scientists interested in methodology
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how to formulate, use, and evaluate scientific hypotheses and the relation between induction, deduction, and verification; includes criteria for when hypothetical reasoning is legitimate. Uses historical examples (Newton, Descartes, undulatory/emission theories, Laplace) to illustrate principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: An hypothesis is any supposition which we make (either without actual evidence, or on evidence avowedly insufficient) in order to endeavor to deduce from it conclusions in accordance with facts which are known to be real.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: to enable deductions that, if true, lend plausibility to the hypothesis. Hypotheses may be about causes, modes of production, or laws of correspondence between co-varying facts. They can be purely conjectural but should aim to lead to testable consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper function of hypotheses (as facilitators of deduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses are invented to enable the Deductive Method to be earlier applied to phenomena and to resolve uniformities into laws of causation from which they can be deductively inferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hypotheses to represent or describe phenomena so that deductive reasoning can produce predictions or explanations; prefer hypotheses allied by analogy to known laws for greater plausibility. Examples: Newton's initial assumption on central force; undulatory vs emission theories of light.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive-method three-part process
rubrics_metrics.description: To discover the cause of any phenomenon by the Deductive Method the process must consist of three parts: induction, ratiocination, and verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: None of the three parts can be dispensed with. Example: Newton's proof identifying gravity with the solar central force involved (1) induction from lunar motions, (2) ratiocination to compute effects for the particular case, (3) verification by comparing calculated effect with observed terrestrial fall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on the Hypothetical Method
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hypothetical Method suppresses the first of the three steps (induction) and contents itself with ratiocination and verification; it is legitimate only if verification amounts to a complete induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimacy requires that a false law cannot lead to the same true result — i.e., the case must be such that no law except the assumed one could give the observed consequences. Otherwise verification alone does not suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for negative instance / exclusivity (Method of Difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a hypothesis to be proved by the hypothetical process it must be possible to obtain both the affirmative and the negative instances required by the Method of Difference so as to show that no antecedent except the assumed one would in conjunction with the background produce the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verification must show not only that AB C produces a b c (affirmative), but also that B C without A does not produce a (negative). Newton's argument is an example: showing no other direction or law of force would accord with Kepler's laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vera causa requirement (testability and detectable cause)
rubrics_metrics.description: A genuinely scientific hypothesis should be of such a nature as to be either proved or disproved by comparison with observed facts; when relating to causation, the supposed cause should be something actually existing or capable of being detected and its influence provable by independent evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The cause need not be already known, but it must be capable in principle of independent detection and proof. If the suggested cause cannot be tested or its existence shown by independent evidence, the hypothesis remains only a plausible conjecture. (Discussed in relation to Newton's maxim and critiques of it.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Unknown-cause hypotheses: provisional utility but weaker status
rubrics_metrics.description: It is allowable and often necessary to begin by asking what unknown cause may have produced an effect, but such hypotheses are provisional and only useful if they suggest a practicable course of investigation that can convert them into testable propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Descartes' vortices would have been legitimate had there been any means of testing them; the vice of the vortex hypothesis was that it could not be conclusively tested. A hypothesis that suggests observations or experiments (thus providing a route to independent evidence) is philosophically acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive success alone does not prove a hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreement of predictions with subsequently observed facts (coincidences between hypothesis and observation) does not, by itself, conclusively prove the reality of the hypothesized cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple successful predictions increase plausibility but do not rule out alternative hypotheses that might also account for the same phenomena. Examples: the undulatory theory of light produced verified predictions (interference), but such success does not prove the reality of an undulatory ether; identity of some laws across phenomena does not imply identity of mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses as indispensable guides to experiment and approximation
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses are indispensable in science for guiding which experiments to try and for enabling the conversion of experimental into deductive truths by tentative assumption and iterative correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with the simplest supposition that accords with obvious facts, trace its consequences, compare with observations, correct the hypothesis, and repeat — analogous to Methods of Approximation in mathematics. Even in experimental science some inducement (a hypothesis) is generally needed to choose difficult or delicate experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity that hypotheses be capable of eventual proof or disproof
rubrics_metrics.description: A condition of the most genuinely scientific hypothesis is that it be not destined always to remain an hypothesis, but be of such a nature as to be either proved or disproved by comparison with observed facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a hypothesis cannot in principle be converted into a proved fact by further observation or experiment, it should be treated as at best a conjecture; it is valuable only insofar as it points to possible independent evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between inventing agencies and inferring past causes
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a difference between inventing agencies to account for classes of phenomena and inferring, in conformity with known laws, what past collocations of known agents produced present effects (as in geology or judicial inquiry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inferring past causes from effects when the agents and laws are known (or no other known cause could account for the effects) is legitimate induction without gratuitous hypothesis. Example: geologists inferring igneous origins from deposits similar to those produced today.

rubrics_metrics.name: Untestable hypotheses are scientifically weak (examples and caveats)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses which cannot lead to any course of investigation capable of converting them from hypothesis into proved fact (or being disproved) are weak and should not be accepted as probably true simply because they account for known phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Descartes' vortices (disproved by cometary passages), the luminiferous ether (currently conjectural; some cosmical variances like Encke's comet might advance it toward testability but do not yet make it conclusive). Such hypotheses may be useful to suggest inquiry but remain conjectural until independent evidence is available.
